PolarQuant: Optimal Gaussian Weight Quantization
via Hadamard Rotation for LLM Compression

Caio Vicentino Email: caiovicentino@proton.me Affiliation: https://github.com/caiovicentino/eoq-quantization
Abstract

We present PolarQuant, a post-training weight quantization method for large language models (LLMs) that exploits the distributional structure of neural network weights to achieve near-lossless compression. PolarQuant operates in three stages: (1) block-wise normalization to the unit hypersphere, (2) Walsh–Hadamard rotation to transform coordinates into approximately Gaussian random variables, and (3) quantization with centroids matched to the Gaussian distribution. Our ablation reveals that Hadamard rotation alone accounts for 98% of the quality improvement, reducing Qwen3.5-9B perplexity from 6.90 (absmax Q5) to 6.40 (Δ=+0.03\Delta=+0.03 from FP16), making it practically lossless without any calibration data. Furthermore, PolarQuant functions as an effective preprocessing step for downstream INT4 quantizers: PolarQuant Q5 dequantized and re-quantized by torchao INT4 achieves perplexity 6.56 versus 6.68 for direct absmax INT4, while maintaining 43.1 tok/s throughput at 6.5 GB VRAM. Code and models are publicly available.

1 Introduction

The deployment of large language models on consumer and edge hardware demands aggressive weight compression. A 9-billion parameter model in FP16 requires approximately 18 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the capacity of most consumer GPUs. Quantization to 4 bits reduces this to roughly 5–6 GB, enabling inference on devices ranging from NVIDIA RTX desktop GPUs to Apple Silicon laptops.

The simplest and most widely deployed quantization scheme is absmax (absolute maximum) quantization [10], which linearly maps values in [−α,α][-\alpha,\alpha] to integer codes, where α=max⁡|wi|\alpha=\max|w_{i}|. While computationally trivial, absmax is provably suboptimal when the weight distribution is non-uniform: it wastes precious codebook entries on rarely occurring outlier magnitudes, and concentrates quantization errors in the high-density central region.

More sophisticated approaches, such as GPTQ [8] and AWQ [11], mitigate this problem through calibration-based Hessian corrections or activation-aware scaling, respectively. NormalFloat (NF4) [7] takes a distributional approach, designing codebooks optimal for normally distributed weights. QuIP# [6] applies random incoherence processing to improve quantization bounds. Recently, TurboQuant [3] demonstrated that normalizing and rotating KV cache vectors via Hadamard transforms yields Gaussian coordinates amenable to optimal quantization.

In this work, we adapt and extend the polar quantization idea from KV cache compression to weight compression. Our key insight is that after block-wise normalization and Hadamard rotation, LLM weight blocks are well-approximated by i.i.d. standard normal random variables, for which the MSE-optimal quantizer is analytically known via the Lloyd–Max algorithm [13, 14]. This yields a quantization scheme that is:

  1. 1.

    Near-lossless. Hadamard rotation alone reduces quantization error by 98%, bringing Q5 perplexity within +0.03+0.03 of FP16 (6.40 vs 6.37) without any calibration data.

  2. 2.

    Simple. The core algorithm is a single matrix multiplication (𝐇128​𝐛^i\mathbf{H}_{128}\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}) per block, with no gradient computation, no iterative optimization, and no calibration data. The Hadamard matrix is deterministic and self-inverse.

  3. 3.

    Composable. PolarQuant serves as a preprocessing step compatible with any downstream quantizer. We demonstrate that PolarQuant Q5 dequantized weights, when re-quantized by torchao INT4 [16], yield 0.12 points lower perplexity than direct absmax INT4 at identical speed and memory.

  4. 4.

    Efficient. The Hadamard matrix is its own inverse (𝐇𝐇⊤=𝐈\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}), requiring no additional storage. Dequantization adds approximately 8 seconds at model load time, with zero runtime overhead.

We evaluate PolarQuant on Qwen3.5-9B [17] and demonstrate state-of-the-art perplexity–compression tradeoffs. Combined with AWQ, PolarQuant achieves a perplexity of 6.43 on WikiText-2 [15], just +0.06+0.06 above FP16, at 3.6×3.6\times compression. On Apple Silicon (Mac mini M4), PolarQuant achieves 19.7 tok/s at 4.8 GB memory with perplexity 6.90.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Absmax Quantization

Given a weight tensor 𝐖\mathbf{W} partitioned into blocks {𝐛i}\{\mathbf{b}_{i}\} of size dd, absmax quantization computes the scale si=maxj⁡|bi,j|s_{i}=\max_{j}|b_{i,j}| and maps each element to the nearest integer in {−2b−1,…,2b−1−1}\{-2^{b-1},\ldots,2^{b-1}-1\}:

qi,j=round⁡(bi,jsi⋅(2b−1−1)).q_{i,j}=\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{b_{i,j}}{s_{i}}\cdot(2^{b-1}-1)\right). (1)

This approach assumes a uniform distribution over [−si,si][-s_{i},s_{i}], which poorly matches the empirically observed near-Gaussian weight distributions [4].

2.2 GPTQ

GPTQ [8] performs layer-wise quantization using approximate second-order (Hessian) information, iteratively quantizing columns and compensating the error in remaining columns via the optimal brain surgeon framework. GPTQ achieves strong results but requires calibration data and is computationally expensive for large models.

2.3 AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization

AWQ [11] observes that a small fraction of weight channels disproportionately affect output quality because they correspond to large activation magnitudes. AWQ computes per-channel scaling factors from calibration activations, protecting important channels from quantization error. We show that AWQ complements PolarQuant: AWQ operates on channels while PolarQuant operates on blocks, and their combination yields near-lossless compression.

2.4 NormalFloat (NF4)

Dettmers et al. [7] introduced NormalFloat, a data type with quantization levels uniformly spaced in the quantile domain of the standard normal distribution. NF4 is information-theoretically optimal when each quantization bin has equal probability. PolarQuant differs in two key ways: (1) we use Lloyd–Max centroids that minimize MSE rather than maximize entropy, and (2) we explicitly transform weights to Gaussian via Hadamard rotation rather than assuming Gaussianity a priori.

2.5 QuIP and QuIP#

QuIP [5] introduced incoherence processing for weight quantization, showing that random orthogonal rotations improve quantization bounds. QuIP# [6] extended this with randomized Hadamard transforms (RHT) and lattice codebooks for 2-bit quantization. While PolarQuant shares the use of Hadamard transforms, our approach differs in two key ways: (1) QuIP# applies rotations to the entire weight matrix columns (inter-block), while PolarQuant applies rotations within each block of 128 elements (intra-block); and (2) QuIP# uses incoherence to bound worst-case error, while PolarQuant uses normalization and rotation to transform the distribution to Gaussian.

2.6 QuaRot and SpinQuant

QuaRot [2] demonstrated that applying Hadamard rotations to hidden states, activations, and KV cache removes outliers without changing model output, enabling outlier-free 4-bit inference. SpinQuant [12] further showed that learned rotation matrices outperform fixed Hadamard rotations by up to 16 points on zero-shot tasks. Both methods apply rotations between layers (requiring graph surgery to absorb rotations into adjacent linear layers), while PolarQuant applies rotations within blocks of each weight tensor independently, requiring no modification to the model graph and enabling use as a simple preprocessing step.

2.7 TurboQuant

TurboQuant [3] applies the polar quantization framework to KV cache compression during inference, normalizing KV vectors, applying random rotation, and quantizing the resulting near-Gaussian coordinates with optimal centroids. TurboQuant proves information-theoretic lower bounds and achieves near-optimal distortion rates. Our work adapts this approach from KV cache to weight compression, demonstrates its effectiveness as a preprocessing step for downstream INT4 quantizers, and provides the first ablation quantifying the individual contributions of rotation (98%) versus optimal centroids (2%) at Q5.

2.8 Lloyd–Max Quantization

The Lloyd–Max algorithm [13, 14] computes the MSE-optimal scalar quantizer for a given source distribution. For a source XX with density f⁡(x)f(x), the optimal quantizer with LL levels satisfies two conditions: (1) each centroid cic_{i} equals the conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[X∣X∈ℛi]\mathbb{E}[X\mid X\in\mathcal{R}_{i}], where ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} is the Voronoi region of cic_{i}; and (2) the boundaries between regions are midpoints of adjacent centroids. For the standard normal distribution, these conditions yield a system of equations with a unique solution [9], which we exploit in section 3.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

PolarQuant quantizes a weight tensor 𝐖∈ℝm×n\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} in four stages:

  1. 1.

    Block decomposition and normalization. Flatten 𝐖\mathbf{W} and partition into blocks {𝐛i}i=1N\{\mathbf{b}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} of size dd (we use d=128d=128). Extract the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm ri=‖𝐛i‖2r_{i}=\left\|\mathbf{b}_{i}\right\|_{2} and normalize: 𝐛^i=𝐛i/ri\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}=\mathbf{b}_{i}/r_{i}.

  2. 2.

    Hadamard rotation. Apply the d×dd\times d normalized Walsh–Hadamard matrix: 𝐛~i=𝐇d​𝐛^i\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i}=\mathbf{H}_{d}\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i}. After rotation, each coordinate is approximately 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d).

  3. 3.

    Scaling and quantization. Scale to unit variance: 𝐳i=d⋅𝐛~i\mathbf{z}_{i}=\sqrt{d}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{i}, so zi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,1)z_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). Quantize each element to the nearest Lloyd–Max centroid c∗=arg​minck⁡|zi,j−ck|c^{*}=\argmin_{c_{k}}|z_{i,j}-c_{k}|.

  4. 4.

    Storage. Store quantized codes (int8), per-block norms (fp16), and centroid table (fp32, shared globally).

Dequantization is the exact inverse: look up centroids from codes, scale by 1/d1/\sqrt{d}, apply inverse Hadamard rotation (since 𝐇d−1=𝐇d\mathbf{H}_{d}^{-1}=\mathbf{H}_{d}), and scale by the stored norm rir_{i}.

3.2 Why Hadamard Rotation Produces Gaussian Coordinates

We now provide the theoretical justification for the Gaussianity of rotated coordinates.

Definition 3.1 (Normalized Walsh–Hadamard Matrix).

The Walsh–Hadamard matrix 𝐇d\mathbf{H}_{d} of order d=2kd=2^{k} is defined recursively:

𝐇1=[1],𝐇2​d=12​[𝐇d𝐇d𝐇d−𝐇d].\mathbf{H}_{1}=[1],\qquad\mathbf{H}_{2d}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H}_{d}&\mathbf{H}_{d}\\ \mathbf{H}_{d}&-\mathbf{H}_{d}\end{bmatrix}. (2)

This matrix is orthogonal (𝐇d​𝐇d⊤=𝐈d\mathbf{H}_{d}\mathbf{H}_{d}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}_{d}) and symmetric (𝐇d=𝐇d⊤\mathbf{H}_{d}=\mathbf{H}_{d}^{\top}), hence self-inverse (𝐇d−1=𝐇d\mathbf{H}_{d}^{-1}=\mathbf{H}_{d}).

Proposition 3.2 (Gaussianity of Rotated Coordinates).

Let 𝐛^∈ℝd\hat{\mathbf{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a random vector uniformly distributed on the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. Let 𝐇d\mathbf{H}_{d} be the normalized Walsh–Hadamard matrix. Then for each coordinate jj, the rotated element b~j=(𝐇d​𝐛^)j\tilde{b}_{j}=(\mathbf{H}_{d}\hat{\mathbf{b}})_{j} satisfies:

d⋅b~j→𝑑𝒩⁡(0,1)as ​d→∞.\sqrt{d}\cdot\tilde{b}_{j}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1)\quad\text{as }d\to\infty. (3)
Proof sketch.

Since 𝐇d\mathbf{H}_{d} is orthogonal, 𝐛~=𝐇d​𝐛^\tilde{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{H}_{d}\hat{\mathbf{b}} is also uniformly distributed on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. Each coordinate of a uniform point on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} has the marginal distribution [9]:

b~j∼1d⋅Beta​(12,d−12)1/2⋅Rademacher,\tilde{b}_{j}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\cdot\text{Beta}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{d-1}{2}\right)^{1/2}\cdot\text{Rademacher}, (4)

which, by the central limit theorem for projections of the sphere, converges to 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) as d→∞d\to\infty. For d=128d=128, the approximation is excellent: the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic between the empirical distribution of rotated LLM weight coordinates and 𝒩⁡(0,1/d)\mathcal{N}(0,1/d) is typically below 0.01. ∎

Remark 3.3.

The practical argument is even stronger than the asymptotic one. Real LLM weight blocks, after normalization, are not exactly uniform on the sphere, but their empirical distributions are sufficiently close that the Gaussian approximation holds well. The Hadamard rotation homogenizes the coordinates: even if the original block has a few large elements (outliers) and many small ones, the rotation spreads the energy across all coordinates, producing a near-Gaussian marginal distribution.

3.3 Lloyd–Max Centroids for the Standard Normal Distribution

Given that rotated and scaled coordinates zi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,1)z_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), the MSE-optimal scalar quantizer with L=2bL=2^{b} levels is obtained by the Lloyd–Max algorithm.

Theorem 3.4 (Lloyd–Max Optimality Conditions).

For a continuous source XX with density f⁡(x)f(x), the MSE-optimal quantizer with levels {c1,…,cL}\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{L}\} and decision boundaries {t0,t1,…,tL}\{t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{L}\} (where t0=−∞t_{0}=-\infty, tL=+∞t_{L}=+\infty) satisfies:

ci\displaystyle c_{i} =𝔼⁡[X∣ti−1<X≤ti]=∫ti−1tix​f​(x)​𝑑x∫ti−1tif⁡(x)​𝑑x,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[X\mid t_{i-1}<X\leq t_{i}]=\frac{\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_{i}}x\,f(x)\,dx}{\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_{i}}f(x)\,dx}, (5)
ti\displaystyle t_{i} =ci+ci+12,i=1,…,L−1.\displaystyle=\frac{c_{i}+c_{i+1}}{2},\quad i=1,\ldots,L-1. (6)

For the standard normal distribution f(x)=ϕ(x)=12​πe−x2/2f(x)=\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}, the centroid condition (5) simplifies to a closed-form expression:

ci=ϕ⁡(ti−1)−ϕ⁡(ti)Φ⁡(ti)−Φ⁡(ti−1),c_{i}=\frac{\phi(t_{i-1})-\phi(t_{i})}{\Phi(t_{i})-\Phi(t_{i-1})}, (7)

where ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) and Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) are the standard normal PDF and CDF, respectively. This follows from the identity ∫abx​ϕ​(x)​𝑑x=ϕ⁡(a)−ϕ⁡(b)\int_{a}^{b}x\,\phi(x)\,dx=\phi(a)-\phi(b).

The Lloyd–Max algorithm iterates between Equations (7) and (6), starting from uniformly spaced boundaries, and converges monotonically in MSE. In practice, convergence to machine precision is achieved within 50 iterations; we use 100 iterations for safety.

Proposition 3.5 (Symmetry).

For the standard normal distribution, the Lloyd–Max quantizer with L=2bL=2^{b} levels is symmetric around zero: ci=−cL+1−ic_{i}=-c_{L+1-i} for all ii.

Proof.

The standard normal density is symmetric (ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(−x)\phi(x)=\phi(-x)), and the Lloyd–Max fixed-point equations preserve this symmetry. By uniqueness of the fixed point, the solution must be symmetric. ∎

Proposition 3.5 halves the storage requirement for the centroid table and simplifies implementation.

Proposition 3.6 (MSE Advantage over Absmax).

Let MSELM\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{LM}} and MSEabs\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{abs}} denote the mean squared quantization errors of the Lloyd–Max and absmax quantizers, respectively, for a 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) source at bb bits. Then:

MSELMMSEabs≤0.46at ​b=3.\frac{\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{LM}}}{\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{abs}}}\leq 0.46\quad\text{at }b=3. (8)

This 54% MSE reduction is the core advantage of PolarQuant over absmax. The improvement arises because absmax places quantization levels uniformly across [−α,α][-\alpha,\alpha], wasting resolution in the tails where the Gaussian density is low, while Lloyd–Max concentrates levels in the high-density central region.

3.4 Algorithm

We present the complete PolarQuant and PolarDequant algorithms.

Complexity. The Walsh–Hadamard transform admits an O⁡(d​log⁡d)O(d\log d) fast implementation (analogous to the FFT), making PolarQuant linear in the number of weights. For d=128d=128, the matrix multiplication 𝐇d​𝐛i\mathbf{H}_{d}\mathbf{b}_{i} via torch.matmul is highly efficient on modern GPUs, completing the entire dequantization of a 9B parameter model in approximately 4 seconds.

Storage overhead. PolarQuant stores one fp16 norm per block of dd elements, adding 16/d=0.12516/d=0.125 bits per weight for d=128d=128. The centroid table (2b2^{b} fp32 values) is shared globally and is negligible.

3.5 PolarQuant + AWQ

AWQ [11] and PolarQuant operate on orthogonal axes: AWQ rescales channels to protect activation-sensitive weights, while PolarQuant normalizes and rotates blocks to enable optimal quantization. Their combination is straightforward:

  1. 1.

    Compute AWQ per-channel scales 𝐬\mathbf{s} from calibration data.

  2. 2.

    Multiply weights by the scales: 𝐖′=𝐖⋅diag⁡(𝐬)\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}).

  3. 3.

    Apply PolarQuant to 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime}.

  4. 4.

    At dequantization, apply inverse AWQ: 𝐖^=𝐖^′⋅diag⁡(𝐬−1)\hat{\mathbf{W}}=\hat{\mathbf{W}}^{\prime}\cdot\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}^{-1}).

This combination reduces the perplexity delta from +0.52+0.52 (PolarQuant Q5 alone) to just +0.06+0.06 (PolarQuant Q5 + AWQ), as shown in section 4.

3.6 PolarQuant as Preprocessing for INT4 Inference

A key contribution of this work is demonstrating that PolarQuant can serve as a preprocessing step that improves the quality of downstream INT4 quantization. The pipeline is:

𝐖→PolarQuant Q5𝐖^PQ→dequant BF16𝐖^BF16→torchao INT4𝐖^INT4.\mathbf{W}\xrightarrow{\text{PolarQuant Q5}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}_{\text{PQ}}\xrightarrow{\text{dequant BF16}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}_{\text{BF16}}\xrightarrow{\text{torchao INT4}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}_{\text{INT4}}. (9)

The intuition is as follows. PolarQuant Q5 with Lloyd–Max centroids produces a dequantized weight 𝐖^BF16\hat{\mathbf{W}}_{\text{BF16}} that has lower MSE to the original 𝐖\mathbf{W} than an absmax Q5 dequantization would. When torchao subsequently re-quantizes this intermediate representation to INT4 using group-wise absmax, it starts from a better approximation of 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The group-wise absmax scale factors computed on 𝐖^BF16\hat{\mathbf{W}}_{\text{BF16}} are more representative of the true weight distribution, because PolarQuant has already removed the outlier-induced distortion.

This is not double quantization in the traditional sense (where both quantization steps are lossy and errors compound). Rather, PolarQuant acts as a denoising step: the Q5 quantization and dequantization effectively project the weights onto a representation that is more amenable to subsequent absmax INT4 quantization.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Model. We evaluate on Qwen3.5-9B [17], a recent 9-billion parameter language model with a hybrid DeltaNet + MoE architecture, chosen for its strong baseline quality and architectural diversity.

Hardware. Primary experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with 96 GB VRAM. Cross-platform experiments use an Apple Mac mini M4 with 16 GB unified memory.

Evaluation. We report perplexity on WikiText-2 [15] using a sliding window of 2048 tokens with stride 512, masking the first 1536 context tokens in each window. This methodology follows the standard established by prior quantization work [8, 11]. All perplexity numbers are deterministic and reproducible.

Speed measurement. Throughput is measured as the average of 3 runs of 100 generated tokens, after a warmup run, in tokens per second (tok/s).

Baselines. We compare against: (1) FP16, the full-precision reference; (2) torchao INT4 [16] with group-wise absmax quantization (group size 128); and (3) BitsAndBytes NF4 [7], the NormalFloat 4-bit format.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 presents the main results on Qwen3.5-9B. PolarQuant Q5 dequantized to FP16 achieves perplexity 6.39 (Δ=+0.02\Delta=+0.02), which is practically lossless without any calibration data. When combined with torchao INT4 for efficient inference, PolarQuant achieves the best perplexity among all INT4 methods (6.56), reducing the gap to FP16 by 39% compared to plain torchao absmax INT4 (from +0.31+0.31 to +0.19+0.19).

Notably, PolarQuant Q5 without AWQ already achieves Δ=+0.02\Delta=+0.02, outperforming PolarQuant+AWQ (Δ=+0.06\Delta=+0.06) which was measured with mixed-bit allocation. This demonstrates that uniform Q5 with Hadamard rotation is superior to mixed-bit allocation with AWQ calibration, a counter-intuitive finding that simplifies the recommended pipeline. In the dequantized FP16 regime, PolarQuant Q5 runs at full FP16 speed (45.9 tok/s) while requiring the same VRAM as FP16 (18.1 GB), making it suitable as a high-fidelity compressed storage and distribution format.

4.3 Cross-Platform Results

To demonstrate portability, we evaluate PolarQuant on Apple Silicon using the MLX framework [1].

PolarQuant enables running a 9B parameter model on a 16 GB consumer device at nearly 20 tokens per second, demonstrating the practical applicability of optimal Gaussian quantization on edge hardware.

4.4 Ablation Study

Table 3 decomposes the contributions of PolarQuant’s two components. The results reveal a striking finding: Hadamard rotation alone accounts for 98% of the improvement, reducing perplexity from 6.90 to 6.40 (Δ=−0.50\Delta=-0.50). Lloyd–Max centroids provide only a marginal additional gain at Q5 (Δ=−0.01\Delta=-0.01), bringing perplexity to 6.39.

This result has an intuitive explanation. At b=5b=5 bits (32 quantization levels), the density of levels is sufficient to approximate the Gaussian distribution well even with uniformly spaced centroids. The dominant source of error is not the centroid placement but rather the mismatch between the weight distribution and the quantizer’s design distribution. Hadamard rotation eliminates this mismatch by transforming the weight distribution to Gaussian, where even a simple uniform quantizer performs near-optimally.

At lower bit widths (e.g., b=2b=2 or b=3b=3), where the few available centroids must be placed carefully, Lloyd–Max centroids would contribute a larger fraction of the improvement. This is consistent with proposition 3.6, which shows 54% MSE reduction at Q3.

A particularly noteworthy result is that PolarQuant Q5 without AWQ already achieves perplexity 6.39, which is lower than PolarQuant+AWQ (6.43) measured in earlier experiments with mixed-bit allocation. This is because uniform Q5 preserves more information than mixed-bit (Q3–Q6) across all layers, confirming that uniform bit allocation with rotation outperforms non-uniform allocation without rotation.

4.5 Version Evolution

Table 4 shows the progressive development of our quantization approach, illustrating the cumulative impact of each technique.

The transition from v1 (absmax) to v3 (PolarQuant + AWQ) reduced the perplexity delta from +0.89+0.89 to +0.06+0.06, a 93% reduction in quantization-induced quality loss.

5 Analysis

5.1 Why PolarQuant Improves Downstream INT4

The central finding of this work is that PolarQuant Q5 dequantized weights, when re-quantized by torchao INT4, yield better perplexity than direct absmax INT4. We offer the following explanation.

Torchao uses group-wise absmax INT4 quantization with group size 128. For each group of 128 weights, it computes s=max⁡|wj|s=\max|w_{j}| and maps all values to 4-bit integers using this scale. The quality of this quantization depends critically on the dynamic range of each group: groups with outliers have large ss and poor resolution for the majority of values.

As our ablation (section 4.4) reveals, the dominant mechanism is Hadamard rotation, which accounts for 98% of the quality improvement. The rotation transforms the weight distribution from a heavy-tailed, non-uniform shape to an approximately Gaussian one. In the Gaussian regime, the dynamic range of each 128-element group is tightly concentrated around 2​ln⁡128≈3.1\sqrt{2\ln 128}\approx 3.1 standard deviations, so the group-wise absmax scale factor closely tracks the true data range. Without rotation, outlier weights inflate the absmax scale, wasting resolution on the tails.

The PolarQuant Q5 dequantized weights have undergone this distributional normalization. When torchao subsequently re-quantizes to INT4, it encounters a weight distribution that is more homogeneous across groups, with fewer outliers and more consistent dynamic range. The result is that each INT4 group achieves better utilization of its 16 available levels.

In essence, PolarQuant acts as a distributional regularizer: Hadamard rotation homogenizes the weight distribution, producing groups that are more amenable to uniform (absmax) quantization.

5.2 The Double Quantization Paradox

One might expect that applying PolarQuant at a lower bit width (e.g., Q3) before torchao INT4 would yield even better results, since the distributional regularization would be stronger. Surprisingly, the opposite is true:

  • •

    Mixed-bit PolarQuant (Q3 for gate/up projections) + torchao INT4: PPL 7.25 (worse)

  • •

    Uniform PolarQuant Q5 + torchao INT4: PPL 6.56 (better)

The explanation is that Q3 dequantization is too lossy: with only 8 centroids, the dequantized weights lose critical fine-grained information that torchao’s INT4 quantizer cannot recover. The optimal operating point requires that the PolarQuant preprocessing preserves enough signal for the downstream quantizer to exploit. At Q5 (32 centroids), the dequantized weights retain sufficient information for torchao to produce a high-quality INT4 representation.

This establishes a principle for cascaded quantization: the preprocessing quantizer must operate at a sufficiently high bit width to preserve the information needed by the downstream quantizer. In our setting, Q5 is the empirically optimal intermediate bit width for a Q5→\toINT4 cascade.

5.3 Computational Overhead

PolarQuant dequantization adds approximately 8 seconds to model load time on the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. This is a one-time cost. At inference time, the computational path is identical to standard FP16 or INT4 inference, with zero additional overhead. The dominant cost during dequantization is the batched matrix multiplication 𝐇128​𝐛^i\mathbf{H}_{128}\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{i} for each block; our implementation uses PyTorch’s torch.matmul, which achieves 25×\times faster execution than a naive fast Walsh–Hadamard transform (FWHT) implementation by leveraging optimized cuBLAS GEMM kernels.

6 Conclusion

We have presented PolarQuant, a simple and effective weight quantization method that achieves near-lossless compression by exploiting the Gaussian structure of Hadamard-rotated weight blocks. Our ablation reveals that the Hadamard rotation is the essential component, accounting for 98% of the quality improvement at Q5. Our key contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Near-lossless compression. PolarQuant Q5 achieves perplexity 6.39 on Qwen3.5-9B (Δ=+0.02\Delta=+0.02 from FP16) without any calibration data, requiring only a single Hadamard matrix multiplication per block.

  2. 2.

    Rotation is the key. Our ablation reveals that Hadamard rotation alone accounts for 98% of the quality improvement (PPL 6.90 →\to 6.40), while Lloyd–Max centroids provide only marginal additional benefit at Q5. This finding simplifies the method to its essential component: a deterministic orthogonal rotation.

  3. 3.

    Improved INT4 inference. When used as a preprocessing step, PolarQuant Q5 + torchao INT4 achieves perplexity 6.56 versus 6.68 for direct absmax INT4, at identical throughput (43.1 tok/s) and near-identical memory (6.5 GB).

  4. 4.

    Cross-platform deployment. PolarQuant runs on both NVIDIA GPUs and Apple Silicon, achieving 19.7 tok/s on a Mac mini M4 at 4.8 GB.

PolarQuant is compatible with any downstream quantizer (torchao, GGUF, MLX) and requires no calibration data for its core algorithm (AWQ is the only component that uses calibration). The method adds no runtime overhead and only a few seconds of one-time dequantization cost at model load.

Limitations and future work. PolarQuant assumes that Hadamard-rotated weight blocks are well-approximated by i.i.d. Gaussians, which may not hold for all architectures. The current implementation does not exploit inter-block correlations. Future work could extend PolarQuant to activation quantization, explore vector quantization with Gaussian codebooks, and investigate the theoretical limits of cascaded quantization pipelines.

Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/caiovicentino/eoq-quantization and https://huggingface.co/caiovicentino1.

Appendix B Mixed-Bit Allocation Strategy

Inspired by Unsloth Dynamic 2.0, we investigated a mixed-bit strategy that assigns different bit widths to different tensor types based on quantization sensitivity:

This achieves a ∼{\sim}3.7-bit average with quality comparable to uniform Q5 at smaller storage. However, as noted in section 5.2, using this mixed-bit scheme as preprocessing for torchao INT4 degrades quality (PPL 7.25) because the Q3 layers lose too much information. The mixed-bit strategy is therefore recommended only for direct PolarQuant inference (without downstream re-quantization).

Appendix D Compression Ratios

Table 7 summarizes the storage requirements and compression ratios for PolarQuant at different bit widths.

The overhead column accounts for per-block norms (fp16, one per 128 elements = 16/128=0.12516/128=0.125 bits per weight). AWQ scales add one fp16 value per channel, which is negligible for large matrices. In the PolarQuant Q5 + torchao INT4 pipeline, the final model uses torchao’s native INT4 format, so the overhead is zero at inference time.
